title: Hershele and the Hungry Shabbat
summary: On Friday night everyone goes home with a guest, and only Hershele is left alone with a tummy that goes grrroo-grrroo. Rich Reb Zalman says there's no room, but Hershele raises a finger: "If you don't invite me, I'll do what my father used to do!" Reb Zalman is so frightened that his table fills up with challah like a pillow, kneidlach like balls and kugel up to the ceiling. A funny rhyming story about Hershele Ostropoler and welcoming guests.
pages:
On Friday night in Ostropol, after the prayers were done,
everyone took a guest home for fish and challah — everyone but one.
Only Hershele was left alone, in the corner by the door,
and his tummy went: grrroo-grrroo! like a cat that yowls for more.

Along came rich Reb Zalman, with a belly big and round,
with a chain of gold and a great fur coat that reached the ground.
Hershele ran up to him: "Reb Zalman, Shabbat Shalom!
Maybe at your table there's a little room?"

Reb Zalman waved his hand: "No room! Go on, go away!"
Hershele raised a finger, squinted one eye — and smiled, as if to say:
"If you don't invite me, Reb Zalman, it'll be bad, it's true...
I'll do what my father used to do!"

Reb Zalman shook like jelly: "Oy! What will he do?
Maybe shout? Maybe smash things? Maybe jump on a chair or two?"
He imagined thunder and lightning, and a cow up on the roof —
"Come, Hershele, come! There's room! And there's fish, too — here's the proof!"

On the table: candles and wine, and a challah big as a pillow, so wide,
and Hershele — nyam, nyam! — ate it all, every crumb inside.
He wiped his mustache: "My father..." — and Reb Zalman cried to his wife, "Yoo-hoo!
More! Bring more! So he won't do what his father used to do!"

Then came gefilte fish, with a carrot on each like a crown on a king,
and soup with kneidlach as big as balls — even bigger than anything!
Hershele sipped: "My father..." — and Reb Zalman was already running with a brand-new pot of stew:
"More! Bring more! So he won't do what his father used to do!"

Roast chicken, and tzimmes — in a pot as big as a bathtub, oh my!
And a kugel tall, so tall, up to the ceiling, up to the attic, sky-high!
Hershele said only "My f—" — and Reb Zalman sprang up like a jack-in-the-box, right on cue:
"More! Bring more! So he won't do what his father used to do!"

And at last — honey cake, and compote with a plum,
and Hershele, round as a drum — boom-boom! — said: "Thank you, that's plenty — not another crumb!"
Reb Zalman scratched his beard and asked in a little whisper, soft and true:
"Well, Hershele, tell me... what did your father used to do?"

Hershele put one hand on his tummy, and one hand on his heart, and said:
"When nobody invited him — my father went hungry to bed!"
Reb Zalman's mouth fell open... then suddenly — ha-ha-ha! — out came a shriek
of laughter, till his fur coat shook, his gold chain bounced, and his chair went creak!

The next Shabbat in Ostropol, after the prayers were done,
Reb Zalman ran over first: "Hershele! Come to us for challah, come!
And bring everyone who's alone — every single one, please do!
So that nobody has to do what your father used to do!"
